newsitem.title: FRANCE: US-Russian ILS wins half of space launch market.
newsitem.headline: US-Russian ILS wins half of space launch market.

text.p: International Launch Services (ILS), the company that launches the U.S. Atlas rocket and Russias Proton, has won half the market in launching heavy satellites and equals its main rival Arianespace, company officials said on Sunday.
ILS, created in 1995, is a joint venture between U.S. aerospace giant Lockheed Martin, Russia's Khrunichev and RSC Enerigia of the Ukraine .
Atlas is launched from the Cape Canaveral, Florida and Proton from the Baikanour Cosmodrome.
ILS officials said its back order stood at 49 satellites to be launched -- 29 for Atlas and 20 for Proton -- worth more than $3 billion.

"ILS has proved to be a remarkable business alliance and perhaps the best example of how American and Russian companies have been able to work together productively... Since June 1995 ILS has managed 15 Atlas launches, extending the record for consecutive successful Atlas launches to 34," Vance Coffman, Lockheed Martin president, told a news conference.

Coffman said ILS plans to introduce more powerful rockets in 1998 capable of launching heavier satellites. A new version of the Atlas will be able to launch four tonnes of payload into geostationary transfer orbit (GTO) -- the orbit used by most heavy communications satellites -- and a new Proton will be able to launch 5.5 tonnes.

"These new vehicles, each of which represents a technical evolution of our proven line of launchers, position ILS to respond quickly to market demand as satellites increase in weight and mass," Coffman said.

For over a decade the Paris-based Arianespace company was undisputed leader in the heavy satellite launch market. Its current satellite backload is now 42 satellites worth an estimated $3.4 billion. The company launches the Ariane-4 rocket series from the European Space Agency (ESA) launch centre in Kourou, French Guiana on the northeast coast of South America.

Arianespace president Charles Bigot disputes ILS's claim to have captured 50 percent of the market. "If we calculated our launch backload the same way as our competitors we would have over 60 launches on schedule. What they (ILS) call a firm contract we would consider an option," Bigot said.
China's launch programme has suffered a spate of recent failures and is no longer considered by many to be a viable player in the market.
McDonnell Douglas Corp launches the flight-proven Delta family of rockets, but cannot launch satellites of the Ariane and ILS weight class.
